title: Liquid AI releases LFM2.5-VL-DSpark, a 280M drafter that speeds vision-language inference 2–3×
subtitle: The Apache-licensed draft model brings multimodal speculative decoding to LFM2.5-VL-3B with less than 9% memory overhead and same-day support in SGLang, llama.cpp and MLX-VLM.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Liquid AI has released LFM2.5-VL-DSpark, an experimental draft model that plugs into the company's existing LFM2.5-VL-3B vision-language model to accelerate inference through speculative decoding. The drafter has roughly 280 million parameters — about 8.9% memory overhead on top of the 3B base — and produces blocks of candidate tokens that the larger model verifies in a single pass. Liquid reports decoding throughput improvements of up to 2.66× on datacenter GPUs and 3.13× on edge devices, with end-to-end throughput gains of 2.27× and 2.62× respectively. The model ships in Safetensors and GGUF via Hugging Face and lists day-one support for SGLang, llama.cpp and MLX-VLM.

Speculative decoding is not new — pairing a small drafter with a large verifier has been standard practice on text-only LLMs for two years — but multimodal is the harder version of the problem. Vision tokens and text tokens have different information density and different verification costs, and drafts that are cheap to generate on the text side tend to miss badly on the image side. DSpark's architectural move is to project visual patches and text tokens into a unified representation before the drafter runs, so a four-layer attention-only network can look at both and produce candidates the verifier will accept at a higher rate. That change is what lets the speedups survive on a workload where images are the main input.

The bigger story is where this runs. Vision-language models on the edge — phones, cameras, robots, medical devices — have been bottlenecked by decoding cost, not by weights. A 3.13× decode speedup on edge hardware is the difference between a model that answers in three seconds and one that answers in one, which is roughly the threshold where a live camera assistant becomes usable rather than experimental. Liquid, spun out of MIT CSAIL, has been positioning around exactly that: efficient models targeted at deployment, not benchmark leaderboards. Apache 2.0 licensing and same-day integration into three popular inference stacks are how you get adopted before larger labs ship a competing pattern.

Takeaway for learners: model release notes lie about what matters. When a lab claims a speedup, read the fine print — is it decode-only throughput, end-to-end latency, or first-token latency? Does the benchmark include the vision encoder? Is the memory overhead the peak or the average? Speculative decoding is a case where the answers actually matter for whether the number you see reproduces on your hardware. If you plan to ship a multimodal product, add a benchmark harness to your CI that measures your workload, not the lab's.
